abstract: |
  Large language models (LLMs) can grade answers to German law exams at scale. But the same answer
  gets different scores from different models, and even from one model on a second run. Some
  examiners grade with a grading sheet (*Bewertungsbogen*) that splits the expected solution into
  small steps worth fixed points. We ask whether a sheet that a model writes from the case and its
  reference solution makes LLM grades steadier, and at what cost to agreement with human graders. A
  first study on 15 exams and 45 human-graded answers used sheets from 12 models. On average the
  sheets did not make the stronger grading models (judges) steadier and tended to lower agreement
  with the human graders. With a sheet, several judges gave high scores to empty answers or to
  answers that only copy the case. In the pipeline we present, one model writes small steps with
  explicit requirements, including paths for defensible alternative solutions and auxiliary opinions
  (*Hilfsgutachten*). The judge must back every point with a quote, and a fixed program checks that
  each quote stands in the answer. On the scripts of one police-law exam, graded on its author's own
  sheet, we test whether sheets make grades steadier and closer to the examiner's, which models write
  and use sheets well, and whether the pipeline meets German examination law. First runs on 15 scripts
  suggest that a sheet does not make repeated runs steadier, but brings the grades much closer to the
  examiner's. \pending{results of the full benchmark and the recommended pipeline}

```{python}
MINUS = "−"


def _q(x, nd):
    """Round half up from the value's decimal form (10.85 -> 10.9), not
    from its binary float (which would give 10.8)."""
    return Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-nd), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)


def num(x, nd=2):
    return f"{_q(x, nd):.{nd}f}".replace("-", MINUS)


def sgn(x, nd=2):
    return f"{_q(x, nd):+.{nd}f}".replace("-", MINUS)


def cor(x, nd=2):
    """Correlations and p-values without the leading zero (.77, -.13)."""
    s = f"{abs(_q(x, nd)):.{nd}f}"
    s = s[1:] if s.startswith("0") else s
    return (MINUS if x < 0 else "") + s


def pv(p):
    return cor(p, 3) if p < 0.01 else cor(p, 2)


def pct(x, nd=0):
    return f"{_q(100 * x, nd):.{nd}f}%"


def ci(c, nd=2):
    """A 95% interval of a difference, in brackets as everywhere in the paper."""
    return f"[{sgn(c[0], nd)}, {sgn(c[1], nd)}]"


def cic(c):
    """A 95% interval of a correlation."""
    return f"[{cor(c[0])}, {cor(c[1])}]"


def rng(a, b, nd=1, sep="–"):
    return f"{num(a, nd)}{sep}{num(b, nd)}"


def usd(x, nd=0):
    return f"USD {x:,.{nd}f}"

def tex_escape(s):
    for a, b in (("\\", "\\textbackslash{}"), ("&", "\\&"), ("%", "\\%"), ("$", "\\$"),
                 ("#", "\\#"), ("_", "\\_"), ("{", "\\{"), ("}", "\\}")):
        s = s.replace(a, b)
    return s


def crit_tex(s):
    return tex_escape(s).replace(">=", "$\\geq$").replace("<=", "$\\leq$").replace("<", "$<$")


def write_table(name, caption, label, header, rows, colspec=None, size=r"\small", wide=False, note=None):
    """A captioned booktabs table in assets/<name>.tex, included with \\input
    (raw blocks with \\caption get mangled by Quarto's crossref pass)."""
    colspec = colspec or ("l" + "r" * (len(header) - 1))
    esc = lambda t: re.sub(r"(?<!\\)%", r"\\%", str(t))  # a bare % would start a LaTeX comment
    caption = esc(caption)
    rows = [r if r == "MIDRULE" else (esc(r) if isinstance(r, str) else [esc(c) for c in r]) for r in rows]
    lines = [r"\begin{table}[t]", rf"\caption{{{caption}}}", rf"\label{{{label}}}", r"\centering", size]
    if wide:
        lines.append(rf"\begin{{tabular*}}{{\textwidth}}{{@{{\extracolsep{{\fill}}}}{colspec}@{{}}}}")
    else:
        lines.append(rf"\begin{{tabular}}{{@{{}}{colspec}@{{}}}}")
    lines += [r"\toprule", " & ".join(header) + r" \\", r"\midrule"]
    for r in rows:
        if r == "MIDRULE":
            lines.append(r"\midrule")
        elif isinstance(r, str):
            lines.append(r + r" \\")
        else:
            lines.append(" & ".join(str(c) for c in r) + r" \\")
    lines += [r"\bottomrule", r"\end{tabular*}" if wide else r"\end{tabular}"]
    if note:
        lines += [r"\par\smallskip", rf"\parbox{{\textwidth}}{{\footnotesize {note}}}"]
    lines.append(r"\end{table}")
    (ASSETS / f"{name}.tex").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("```{=latex}\n\\input{assets/" + name + ".tex}\n```\n")
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

German law students learn and are examined through case solutions (*Falllösungen*). A candidate
receives a fact pattern (*Sachverhalt*) and writes a legal opinion in a prescribed appraisal style
(*Gutachtenstil*), which the state examinations grade on a statutory scale from 0 to
`{python} V["R18"]` grade points [@jurprnotskv1981]. Different examiners often give the same answer
different grades [@hufeld2024]. Some correctors therefore first note what each part of the expected
solution is worth [@frenzel2011korrektur, p. 330], and a few examiners make this binding in a grading
sheet (*Bewertungsbogen*) [@heidebach2015pruefen; @strecker2026ki]. Such a sheet splits the expected
solution into small steps, each worth some assessment units (*Bewertungseinheiten*, BE), and a key
maps the BE total to a grade. Appendix \ref{sec-app-glossary} lists the German and the technical terms
we use.

Large language models (LLMs) can grade such texts at scale; an LLM used as a grader is called a
*judge*. On German case solutions, a judge that applies the same `{python} V["n_dims"]` general
criteria to every exam stays within the range of human disagreement, but its scores vary between
judges and between repeated runs [@nagl2026bengerdata]. For candidates this is a matter of equal
opportunity (*Chancengleichheit*), since comparable candidates must be graded by comparable standards
[@bverfge84_34, p. 52]. We test the examiners' remedy: one model, the *generator*, writes an
exam-specific grading sheet from the case and its reference solution (*Musterlösung*), and the judge
grades against it. The sheet also gives the examiner a document to read and correct.

Study 1 tested this remedy on `{python} V["n_exams"]` exams with `{python} V["n_answers"]` answers and
blind human grades. On average the sheets did not make the stronger judges steadier and tended to
lower agreement with the human graders. With a sheet, several judges also gave high scores to empty
answers or to answers that only copy the case (@sec-first). The pipeline we present (@sec-pipeline) is
designed against these failures. Study 2 tests it on the written answers (*scripts*) to a police-law
exam set by one of us and graded on the author's own sheet and key, and it asks what German
examination law requires of such grading. Four research questions guide the paper:

- **RQ1 Variance.** Does a generated sheet make LLM grades steadier than grading without one, counting
  the scatter between runs, judges and the sheets one generator may write? Does it beat averaging
  several runs at equal cost?
- **RQ2 Validity.** How close are sheet-based grades to the examiner's and to a second human grader,
  and how many students would they wrongly pass or fail?
- **RQ3 Generators and judges.** Which models write sheets that yield grades close to the examiner's
  at low cost, and which judges use them well?
- **RQ4 Law.** Does sheet-based grading meet what German examination law asks of grading, on
  defensible (*vertretbar*) alternative solutions, follow-on errors (*Folgefehler*), reasons for each
  point and equal opportunity, and which uses does the evidence support?

Our contributions are:

1. A pipeline that turns doctrine into checkable structure (@sec-pipeline): steps with explicit
   requirements, separate paths for defensible alternative solutions, owed auxiliary opinions
   (*Hilfsgutachten*), and points only for quotes that a fixed program finds in the answer.
2. A study of all scripts of one exam that splits the scatter of grades into its sources (runs,
   judges, sheets) and compares sheets with averaging runs at equal cost (RQ1).
3. Agreement with the examiner, a second human grader and the examiner's own second grading,
   counting the students an LLM would wrongly pass or fail (RQ2), and a small benchmark of generators
   and judges (RQ3).
4. A legal analysis, co-written with the exam's author, that maps each requirement of examination law
   to a design feature and a test (@sec-practice, RQ4).

# Grading practice in German law exams {#sec-practice}

\draftnote{to be co-written with the exam author; every pending item below needs the author's input or experiments E2, E4 and E5}

*The setting.* The statutory scale has `{python} V["bands"]` grades (*Notenstufen*) from 0 to
`{python} V["R18"]` grade points, and `{python} V["pass_np"]` points (*ausreichend*, "sufficient") is
the lowest grade that still meets average requirements despite its flaws [@jurprnotskv1981, § 1]. In
practice a single exam is passed from this grade, although the rules on passing are state (*Land*)
law. Examiners set their own standards for an exam and must apply them to every script alike
[@bverwg2018_6B71_17]. University exams usually have one grader [@strecker2026ki, p. 29]; some
correctors first build a private point scheme [@frenzel2011korrektur, p. 330], and a few examiners
make it binding in a sheet [@heidebach2015pruefen], but such sheets are rare [@strecker2026ki, p. 3].
Two principles bind any sheet. A defensible solution (*vertretbare Lösung*), consistently argued with
weighty reasons, must not be marked as wrong, which for exams that control access to a profession
follows from Art. 12(1) GG [@bverfge84_34, p. 55]. And a follow-on error (*Folgefehler*) should cost
points only once, so a later step that correctly builds on the candidate's own earlier decision still
earns credit. \pending{exam author: source for the follow-on-error principle}

*Three paradigms.* We compare three ways of grading with our sheet (Table \ref{tab:paradigms} in
Appendix \ref{sec-app-paradigms}). The exam author's sheet (D2) is a list of steps with absolute BE,
grouped into sections. Gregor Roth's sheet for a civil-law exam (Z2) is a tree in which each item
carries a percentage of the item above it. Each of the `{python} Z2["weighted_leaves"]` smallest items
gets a grade from `{python} num(Z2["leaf_grade_range"][0], 0)` to
`{python} num(Z2["leaf_grade_range"][1], 0)`, and the final grade is their average weighted by these
percentages, so the method needs no key [@strecker2026ki, p. 12]. A third practice is common as well:
about `{python} pct(PF["fixed_share"])` of the BE go to steps, and the grader distributes the remaining
`{python} pct(PF["free_share"])` freely, for instance for structure or the overall impression. We do
not adopt it, because the free share is tied to nothing in the answer that a second grader or a judge
could check, so it invites variance and cannot be reproduced. Our sheet follows the first paradigm:
every BE, in half points, belongs to a step, each step lists the requirements that earn it, and code
does all arithmetic (@sec-pipeline).

*Q1: How should the BE be distributed?* The author's sheet spreads `{python} D2["sheet"]["total_be"]`
BE over `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_steps"]` steps with at most `{python} num(D2["sheet"]["max_step_be"], 0)`
BE per step, and some step weights changed between years (@sec-d2) \pending{exam author: why}. We took
the step-size guidance of our generator (`{python} num(GEN["step_be_guidance"][0], 1)` to
`{python} num(GEN["step_be_guidance"][1], 0)` BE per step, at most `{python} num(GEN["max_step_be"], 0)`
BE) from the two expert sheets, so step size is an input of our design, not a finding. E3 compares the
BE distributions of generated sheets with the author's sheet and E5 with Roth's. \pending{BE
distribution of the expert sheet and of generated sheets (E3)}

*Q2: What earns credit, including method?* In the author's sheet every step credits an issue spotted
or an argument made. No step credits a bare result, although some step titles state a sub-result. Our
generator follows the same rule: a result earns credit only with the reasoning that carries it, and
where several results are defensible, the requirements credit the argument [@bverfge84_34, p. 55].
The exam author credits method (structure, appraisal style, precise language) inside each section
rather than as a separate block [@strecker2026ki, p. 14]. \pending{exam author: confirm for D2}

*Q3: Where is the pass mark?* The author's key passes a script at
`{python} pct(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"])` of the BE. Where the pass mark lies is part of the examiner's
own evaluation; it cannot be fixed rigidly without regard to average results [@bverfge84_34, p. 51],
and once set it applies to every script alike [@bverwg2018_6B71_17]. The mark decides which students
a judge passes or fails differently from the examiner, and E2 sweeps it from
`{python} pct(EXP["E2"]["pass_mark_sweep"][0])` to `{python} pct(EXP["E2"]["pass_mark_sweep"][1])` on
stored outputs. \pending{E2}

*Q4: Is the key linear or curved?* The author's key is piecewise linear with a kink at the pass mark:
below it a grade point spans `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_below_pass"]` BE, and from the
pass mark upwards `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_from_pass"]` BE, up to grade 18 at
`{python} D2["sheet"]["key_top_grade_be"]` BE. The same shape, with passing costing more BE per grade
than the top grades, is proposed in [@strecker2026ki, p. 15]. \pending{exam author: confirm the
reasons for D2} Roth's paradigm needs no key, since it averages statutory grades and passes from
grade `{python} Z2["workbook"]["pass_from_grade"]`.

*Q5: How are cardinal errors treated?* A cardinal error (*Kardinalfehler*) is one that by itself can
make a script fail. Examiners disagree on what counts, and the literature asks each sheet to define
it in advance, with minus points or a grade cap [@strecker2026ki, pp. 15 f.]. \pending{exam author:
examples and expected loss for D2} Our sheet has no such cap yet; the follow-on-error rule and the
standard of each requirement decide how far an early error carries (@sec-judge). E4 tests
`{python} EXP["E4"]["kardinalfehler_probes"]` fake answers with the losses the author expects.

# Related work {#sec-related}

*Grading with LLMs.* A judge reads an answer and returns a score. Such judges agree with human
graders on average [@zheng2023mtbench; @liu2023geval] but are less dependable on a single answer. The
same answer can get a different score when graded again [@haldar2025rating; @schroeder2024trust],
scores change when answers are shown in another order [@wang2024fair; @shi2024judging], and judges
favour texts written by their own model [@panickssery2024self]. A grader can also be steady and still
wrong [@jade2026chatgpt; @xue2026consistency], so each use must be checked against human graders
[@gu2024survey; @bavaresco2025llms; @calderon2025alternative]. Testing research splits score
differences into parts due to the student, the grader and the occasion (generalizability theory)
[@brennan2001generalizability]; this has been applied to LLM graders [@song2026exploring;
@wang2025evaluating], and the wording of the grading prompt has been treated as one such part
[@messing2026hidden]. Most fixes change the grader, for example by pooling several models
[@verga2024replacing]. We change the sheet the grader uses, and we count the sheet a model happens to
write as a source of differences of its own.

*Grading sheets written by models.* A rubric is a scoring guide that states what earns credit, and a
checklist breaks it into yes-or-no items. Such items can make LLM grading more consistent
[@ye2024flask; @kim2024prometheus; @lee2025checkeval; @cook2024ticking; @chen2026holistic], and rubrics
written for one question work better than general ones [@jonsson2007use; @pathak2025rubric;
@tang2026designing]. Human graders, too, agree more when they score an answer part by part than when
they form one overall impression, at a cost in time [@klein1998analytic]; for an LLM, the time becomes
computing cost. Models can write such rubrics: they derive weighted criteria from a reference answer
[@gunjal2025rubrics; @fan2024sedareval; @li2026rubrichub] and point schemes for exam questions and
proofs [@golchin2025grading; @xie2025grade; @mahdavi2025refgrader; @ma2026proofbench]. Generated
rubrics still fall short of expert ones [@zhou2026rubricbench; @wu2026unveiling], and a regenerated
marking scheme graded less accurately than the one the human graders had used [@ma2026proofbench].
Because models that add up points themselves make mistakes [@kortemeyer2024grading;
@pires2025automatic], our generator states only relative weights and code allocates the points. Our
sheet also encodes two rules of examination law: defensible alternative solutions, and follow-on
errors that cost points only once.

*Evidence and gaming.* Attribution research asks whether a text is backed by the sources it cites
[@rashkin2023measuring; @gao2023alce], and some systems require exact quotes and check them in code
[@menick2022gophercite; @khan2024debating; @hong2026rulers]. Automated scoring has long been open to
gaming by padding, nonsense or keyword lists [@powers2002stumping; @ding2020dont], and LLM graders can
be steered by instructions hidden in an answer [@chiang2024large; @li2026important]. Our judge must
quote the answer for every credit, code removes a credit whose quote is missing or turned into its
opposite, and fake answers test every judge before use.

*Grading law exams.* Research first asked whether LLMs pass law exams [@choi2023chatgpt;
@katz2024gpt4; @martinez2025reevaluating] and now asks whether they can grade them. The graders
receive model answers, marked passages, or rubrics written by experts or exam offices
[@fan2026lexam; @chlapanis2025greekbarbench; @shi2026plawbench; @pires2025automatic;
@pires2026magisbench; @cope2026grading; @akarajaradwong2026thai], while others split answers into
single legal points [@enguehard2025lemaj] or derive issue trees from court judgments [@lee2026legit].
German examiners disagree widely [@hufeld2024]. An examiner's own point scheme cut the spread between
human correctors by almost half [@strecker2026ki], and LLM grades have been validated against the same
examiner's grades on the examiner's own scheme [@zubaer2026gradelegal]. To our knowledge, no study on
law exams has a model write the point scheme from the reference solution, with scoreable paths for
defensible alternatives and a follow-on-error standard per requirement, and tests the result against
the examiner's own sheet and grades.

# The pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

Figure \ref{fig:pipeline} shows the pipeline. Models do two things only: the generator writes the
sheet and says how much each part weighs, and the judge grades an answer against the sheet and quotes
the answer for every credit. Plain code, a fixed program rather than a model, does everything that can
be computed or checked. Since models that add up points themselves make mistakes
[@kortemeyer2024grading; @pires2025automatic], no model ever states points.


## Generation: the checklist sheet {#sec-generation}

The generator receives the case text, the reference solution and fixed instructions, the same for
every model (Appendix \ref{sec-app-spec}), and returns a *checklist sheet* with these parts:

- *Sections and steps.* Each step names one expected legal performance and carries a relative
  weight. The exam's focal problems (*Klausurschwerpunkte*) are marked groups of steps, and each step
  belongs to a work result (*Arbeitsergebnis*), such as an opinion or a draft judgment.
- *Requirements.* Each step lists `{python} GEN["bullets_per_step"][0]` to
  `{python} GEN["bullets_per_step"][1]` requirements, each with a share of the step and a standard
  (*Maßstab*). A requirement is either correct (*richtig*), judged against the correct law, or
  consistent (*folgerichtig*), judged against the candidate's own earlier decision; the latter carries
  the follow-on-error rule. Each requirement names something the answer must write, which a quote can
  show. None may be met by leaving something out, none may be conditional, and none may ask only for
  a norm, a term or a result.
- *Forks and alternative paths.* A dispute that changes only a result or its reasons stays inside one
  step, and its requirement credits the argument whatever the result. A structural fork
  (*Weichenstellung*) exists only where another defensible decision removes or adds steps; each
  alternative path (*Lösungsweg*) then has its own steps, its defensibility requirements
  (*Vertretbarkeitsanforderungen*), and the same BE as the steps it replaces.
- *Auxiliary opinions* (*Hilfsgutachten*). A step can be marked as owed even when the candidate's own
  decision cuts it off, for instance when a contractual claim already fails at formation.

The model states weights, never points.

## Points, checks and grades by code {#sec-allocation}

Code turns the weights into `{python} GEN["total_be"]` BE in half points, using the largest-remainder
method known from seat allocation (Hamilton, in Germany Hare-Niemeyer) [@balinski2001fair]: each step
first gets the whole half points its weight earns, and the leftover half points go to the steps with
the largest remainders. Every step gets at least `{python} num(GEN["min_step_be"], 1)` BE, and a
heavier step never gets fewer points than a lighter one. A requirement is worth its share of the step,
and an alternative path is worth the steps it replaces.

A program, the *validator*, then checks the sheet against fixed rules (Appendix
\ref{sec-app-validator}). Hard rules cover the structure, every cross-reference, the rules for
requirements and forks, and the cap of `{python} num(GEN["max_step_be"], 0)` BE per step. If one fails,
the generator gets its sheet back with the error messages and tries again, up to
`{python} GEN["max_attempts"]` times, whereas soft rules only log a warning. The rules compare words,
so two steps that say the same thing in other words both pass. Every sheet records the hashes of the
validator and of the instructions.

At the end, code adds up the credited points, rounds the total once to half points and maps it to a
grade with the exam's key; several runs can be averaged.

## Judging {#sec-judge}

Code formats the sheet as text for the judge, which receives the case, the reference solution, the
sheet and the answer, each clearly marked, and answers in a fixed format. We test two scoring units.
In the *requirement* unit the judge marks each requirement as met, partly met or not met, which earns
`{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["2"], 0)`, `{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["1"], 1)` or
`{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["0"], 0)` times its BE. In the *step* unit it awards each step up
to its BE in half points, as on a classic sheet. Every credit needs a word-for-word quote from the
answer, and the judge follows fixed rules:

- *Placement.* Work counts once, for the step whose requirement it meets, even if it stands elsewhere
  in the same question and work result. Work on another question counts only if the answer refers to
  it.
- *Follow-on errors.* Requirements with the consistent standard are judged on the answer's own
  earlier decisions. Other requirements are judged on the correct law, but an error that has already
  cost points is not charged again.
- *Auxiliary opinions.* Work on questions that the answer's own decision cut off earns credit like
  work in the main opinion, but it never replaces the main result.
- *Alternatives.* The judge scores the steps of every path and names, with a quote, the path the
  answer follows. A path counts only if the answer gives the reasons its defensibility requirements
  demand, and code counts the named path (design A2).

Further rules cover unforeseen paths, contradictions and padding (Appendix \ref{sec-app-alternatives}),
which also describes the two other designs for alternative paths that E4 compares. The judge is told to
ignore instructions inside its inputs, which a fake answer tests, and it writes short feedback for the
candidate that never changes points.

## The quote check and its limits {#sec-verifier}

Code checks that every quote really stands in the answer (Appendix \ref{sec-app-verifier}). It
tolerates small differences in layout, inflection and typing, but words that change the meaning must
match exactly: negations, result words such as *rechtmäßig* and *rechtswidrig* (lawful, unlawful),
qualifiers and numbers. A quote also fails if a negation or a condition stands right next to it, and a
credit whose quote fails is set to zero.

The check has limits. It tests that a quote exists, not that it proves the requirement, so a real
sentence can be quoted for the wrong requirement. Correct work that the judge paraphrases earns
nothing, a sentence copied from the case text passes, and the strict rules at the edges also reject
some correct quotes.
\pending{regression replays at the freeze: quotes re-checked on D1 and D2, and how many flip}

## D1: the BenGER exams {#sec-d1}

D1 holds the `{python} V["n_exams"]` exams of the BenGER corpus [@nagl2026bengerdata]. All four
graders used the prior study's `{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria, which its LLM judge also used.
The blind graders often disagree: their highest and lowest grade for an answer lie
`{python} V["spread"]` points apart on average. @sec-first compares with the mean of all
`{python} V["pool"]` grades on the `{python} V["n_ann"]` answers written by people, as the prior study
did, whereas E2 uses the blind grades as the main reference and the creator's grade as a second one.
The prior study's judge was `{python} V["prior_mae"]` points (`{python} V["prior_mae_np"]` grade
points) from the mean human grade on average and ranked the answers much as the humans did ($r$ =
`{python} V["prior_r"]`). D1 is our only data across many exams, but its reference is noisy.

## D2: the expert exam {#sec-d2}

D2 is one police-law exam from LMU, set each year from 2024 to 2026, whose author is a co-author of
this paper. The author's sheet has `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_steps"]` steps worth
`{python} D2["sheet"]["total_be"]` BE in half points, and the author's key passes a script at
`{python} pct(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"])`. Some step weights changed between years, so the sheet
exists in `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_states"]` versions with the same steps; the judge always sees the
current one.

- *D2a* holds `{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` typed scripts, `{python} D2["d2a"]["by_year"]["2024"]`
  from 2024 and `{python} D2["d2a"]["by_year"]["2025"]` from 2025, graded step by step on the sheet
  version then in use. We call these *reference grades*, because for
  `{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` scripts the grader is still being confirmed.
- *D2b* holds `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_students"]` student scripts from 2026, written on our platform as
  a practice exam; we drop `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_excluded"]` uploads from the author's own account (a
  test upload and a copy of a D2a script). The platform graded the scripts on submission with GPT-5.4
  Mini, and the students saw these grades. The author grades them blind, without seeing any model
  grade. \pending{blind expert grades for D2b}

D2 thus has `{python} D2["distinct_scripts"]` distinct scripts, or
`{python} D2["n_counting_dependent_pair_once"]` if one pair that shares text counts once. We lack the
2024 case text, so the `{python} D2["d2a"]["later_case_text"]` scripts of 2024 are judged against a
later one. \pending{the 2024 case text from the exam author}

All D2 texts were pseudonymized and checked for personal data before any research call to a model
provider (Appendix \ref{sec-app-datastatement}). No generator and no judge without a sheet sees the
author's sheet, and a canary check confirms that the fixed instructions and examples in every prompt
contain no terms from the author's sheet or exam.

*Z2* is Gregor Roth's sheet and grading workbook for a civil-law exam, so far without case, reference
solution or scripts. E5 generates sheets for this exam and compares them with Roth's sheet.
\pending{case and reference solution from Roth}

## Experiments {#sec-experiments}

D1 and D2a are development data. D2b is held out: it holds new scripts of the same exam, not a new
exam, which the author grades from exported files before seeing any generated sheet or model grade,
and one registered test runs on them once. \pending{the registered hypothesis and its success
criterion} Stability needs no human grade, so E1 uses all `{python} D2["distinct_scripts"]` D2
scripts. Table \ref{tab:experiments} lists the experiments. The baselines are grading without a sheet,
on the prior study's `{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria, and grading on the exam author's own
sheet. Since the author's sheet has no requirements, the judge scores it per step, whereas generated
sheets are scored both ways so that the sheet and the scoring unit can be told apart. The whole
program costs `{python} usd(COST["experiments_sum_usd"][0])` to `{python} COST["experiments_sum_usd"][1]`
at list prices (Appendix \ref{sec-app-datastatement}).

```{python}
#| output: asis
erows = [[e["id"], e["name"], ", ".join(e["rq"]), tex_escape(e["scope"])] for e in DZ["experiments"]]
write_table(
    "tbl_experiments", "Experiments of Study 2. \\pending{actual costs per experiment}",
    "tab:experiments", ["", "Experiment", "RQ", "What we do"], erows,
    colspec="lp{0.16\\textwidth}p{0.1\\textwidth}p{0.6\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

*Measures.* Accuracy is the average distance of a total from the human grade (mean absolute error,
MAE) and its sign (bias: too generous or too strict). We also give the error in grade points on the 0
to `{python} V["R18"]` scale and the number of students a model passes or fails differently from the
human grade. For stability we split the spread of totals into real differences between scripts and
noise from the judge, from the sheet a generator happens to write and from repeated runs
[@brennan2001generalizability]. Dependability, from 0 to 1, is the share of the spread that reflects
real differences between scripts when a single run decides. We also count how often a second run
lands on the other side of the pass mark [@livingston1995estimating] and compare sheets with averaging
runs at equal cost. Each human reference was graded with one method, D1 on the `{python} V["n_dims"]`
general criteria and D2 on the author's sheet, so each favours the grading basis it shares.

*Fake answers (probes).* Before any benchmark run, every judge and sheet must clear a set of fake
answers in each of `{python} DZ["probes"]["passes"]` runs (Appendix \ref{sec-app-probes}): empty,
copied, off-topic or manipulative answers must score about zero, and the reference solution must score
high. Cutting one section of the reference solution must cost about its BE, while moving correct
reasoning under another heading should cost almost nothing.

*Uncertainty.* Apart from the registered test, we estimate rather than test. Every range is a 95%
interval from redrawing exams (D1) or scripts (D2) many times (bootstrap), and with
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` graded scripts only large differences are visible (Appendix
\ref{sec-app-precision}). Each judge runs at one fixed temperature in all comparisons, and scripts that
the judge flags for review keep their totals in our analyses.

# Results {#sec-results}

Totals are points out of 100, and a grade point is one step on the 0 to `{python} V["R18"]` scale. On
the expert exam, `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_from_pass"]` points make one grade point from
the pass mark (`{python} num(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"] * D2["sheet"]["total_be"], 0)` points) up and
`{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_below_pass"]` below it. $r$ says whether two graders rank the
scripts in the same order (1 = the same order) and ignores a constant shift. Brackets give 95%
intervals; if the interval of a difference includes zero, we cannot tell whether the difference is
real.

## Study 1: a step-score sheet on 15 exams {#sec-first}

```{python}

llama = "meta-llama/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-FP8"

opus, sonnet = "claude-opus-4-7", "claude-sonnet-4-6"

lz, lf, lfz, mz = CO["luna_zs_vs_hol"], CO["luna_fs_vs_hol"], CO["luna_fs_vs_zs"], CO["mini_zs_vs_hol"]
pooled = CO["pooled_five"]
son_f, mini_f = per_judge_forest[sonnet], per_judge_forest[MINI]
fs_sd = CO["fewshot_per_generator_repeat_sd"]
roster = {r["judge"]: r for r in JU["roster"]}
extra = {r["judge"]: r for r in JU["extra_single_pass"]}
gpo = GE["per_generator"]

fc = PR["fail_counts"]
npas = PR["n_passes"]

gen_s = G["per_generator"]
prs = FI["reliability"]["panel_sd_range"]
six = statistics.fmean(f["delta"] for f in CO["per_judge"])
mini_ci_has_zero = mini_f["ci95"][0] < 0 < mini_f["ci95"][1]
```

Study 1 tested a step-score sheet on D1, in which each step carried a weight class, ordered levels of
partial credit and follow-on-error rules. `{python} V["n_gens"]` generators wrote one sheet per exam,
and a random draw picked one sheet per exam for all judges. `{python} len(JU["roster"])` judges graded
the `{python} V["n_answers"]` answers `{python} passes` times with that sheet
(`{python} len(JU["extra_single_pass"])` more once), and `{python} len(CO["per_judge"])` of them also
graded without a sheet, on the prior study's `{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria
[@nagl2026bengerdata]. Totals are sums of the step scores (Appendix \ref{sec-app-first}).

*Writing sheets worked.* `{python} V["n_valid"]` of `{python} V["n_cells"]` pairs of generator and
exam yielded a valid sheet, and `{python} V["n_full"]` of the `{python} V["n_gens"]` generators
covered every exam, but the sheets differed widely: the mean number of steps per generator ranged from
`{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][0], 0)` to `{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][1], 0)`
(Table \ref{tab:compliance}).

*The sheets did not make grading steadier* (Table \ref{tab:reliability}). Graded again, Luna's total
for the same answer moved by `{python} num(REL["holistic_luna"]["repeat_sd"], 1)` points without a
sheet and `{python} num(REL["tailored_luna"]["repeat_sd"], 1)` with one (standard deviation over runs).
Across the `{python} pooled["n_judges"]` judges other than GPT-5.4 Mini, the sheet changed this spread
by `{python} sgn(pooled["point"])` points on average `{python} ci(pooled["ci95"])`, and Claude Sonnet
4.6 was steadier without a sheet (Table \ref{tab:contrasts}); with GPT-5.4 Mini included, the average
would be `{python} sgn(six)`. GPT-5.4 Mini's own spread grew from
`{python} num(REL["holistic_mini"]["repeat_sd"], 1)` to `{python} num(REL["tailored_mini"]["repeat_sd"], 1)`
points`{python} ", although its interval includes no change" if mini_ci_has_zero else ""`. The judges
disagreed with one another far more than with themselves: the standard deviation of the
`{python} FI["reliability"]["panel_size"]` judges' totals for the same answer was
`{python} num(prs[0], 0)` to `{python} num(prs[1], 0)` points.

*Nor did the sheets bring the grades closer to the humans.* With the sheet, Luna ranked the answers
about as before ($r$ = `{python} cor(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])` against
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["hol"]["r"])`) but turned from `{python} num(AG["luna"]["hol"]["bias"], 0)`
points too generous to `{python} num(abs(REL["tailored_luna"]["bias"]), 0)` points too strict, and
GPT-5.4 Mini's average error rose from `{python} num(AG["mini"]["hol"]["mae"], 0)` to
`{python} num(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 0)` points.

*The sheets invited credit for nothing.* With a sheet, Luna gave a near-empty answer about
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["tailored"], 0)` of 100 points in
`{python} fc["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` of `{python} npas["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` runs and
`{python} "never did so without one" if fc["holistic"][LUNA]["empty"] == 0 else "rarely without one"`,
while GPT-5.4 Mini gave empty answers a median of
`{python} num(sev["tailored"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)` points. Only
`{python} " and ".join(NAME[j] for j in PR["clean_battery"])` kept every fake answer near zero on
every run (Table \ref{tab:probes}).

We attribute these failures mainly to the Study 1 pipeline, which checked no quotes, listed the steps
out of outline order and gave the steps of alternative paths no fields of their own (Appendix
\ref{sec-app-corrections}). The pipeline of Section \ref{sec-pipeline} checks every quote, keeps the
outline order and gives every path its own fields, and E0 and E3 test whether weaker judges can then
use a sheet safely.

```{python}
def _v(arm, judge):
    return ((VAL2 or {}).get("per_arm", {}).get(arm, {}) or {}).get(judge)


def _c(a, b):

        if (c["a"]["judge"], c["a"]["arm"]) == a and (c["b"]["judge"], c["b"]["arm"]) == b:
            return c
    return None


def _d(x, nd=1):
    """A paired difference with its bootstrap interval."""
    return f"{sgn(x['mean_diff'], nd)} [{sgn(x['ci95'][0], nd)}, {sgn(x['ci95'][1], nd)}]"


def RP(w):
    """A right-aligned paragraph column of width w (share of the text width)."""
    return r">{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{%.2f\textwidth}" % w


def _n1(v):
    """One decimal, without a trailing .0 (counts averaged over runs)."""
    t = num(v, 1)
    return t[:-2] if t.endswith(".0") else t


def _wrong(x):
    return f"{_n1(x['wrong_pass'])} / {_n1(x['wrong_fail'])}"


def val_table(name, label, arms, extra):
    rows = []
    for arm, lbl in arms.items():
        per = (VAL2 or {}).get("per_arm", {}).get(arm, {})
        for j in JUDGES_ORDER:
            x = per.get(j)
            if not x:
                continue
            c = x.get("mae_ci95") or [None, None]
            gated = (GATE2 or {}).get("batteries", {}).get(arm, {}).get(j)
            mark = "$^\\dagger$" if not gated else ("" if gated["battery"] == "pass" else "$^\\ddagger$")
            rows.append([lbl, SHORT.get(j, NAME.get(j, j)) + mark, str(x["complete_passes"]),
                         num(x["mae"], 1) + (f' [{num(c[0], 1)}, {num(c[1], 1)}]' if c[0] is not None else ""),
                         num(x["mae_grade_points"], 1), sgn(x["bias"], 1), cor(x["pearson"]), _wrong(x),
                         num(x["mean_abs_pass_diff"], 1) if x.get("mean_abs_pass_diff") is not None else "--"])
    write_table(
        name,
        f"Expert exam: judge totals against the reference grades of the {D2['d2a']['n_scripts']} D2a scripts, in "
        f"points out of 100 (from the pass mark of {num(VAL2['pass_mark_be'], 0) if VAL2 else ''} points up, "
        f"{D2['sheet']['key_be_per_grade_from_pass']} points make one grade point). {extra}Each value is computed "
        "per run and averaged over the runs. Grade points: the average error on the 0 to 18 scale under the "
        "exam's key. Wrongly passed: students the judge passes whom the reference fails, and wrongly failed the "
        "reverse. Run to run: the average difference between two runs on the same script. "
        "$^\\dagger$ not checked with the fake answers. $^\\ddagger$ failed that check (Table \\ref{tab:gate2}).",
        label,
        ["Grading basis", "Judge", "Runs", "Average error [95\\%]", "Grade points", "Generous (+), strict ($-$)",
         "$r$", "Wrongly passed / failed", "Run to run"],
        rows or [[r"\tbd"] * 9],
        colspec="p{0.28\\textwidth}lr" + "".join(RP(w) for w in (0.12, 0.06, 0.09)) + "r" + RP(0.08) + RP(0.05),
        size=r"\scriptsize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}")


LV = ((VAR2 or {}).get("per_judge", {}) or {}).get(LU, {})


def stab_table(name, label, only_full):
    rows = []
    inst = LV.get("instruments") or {}
    gens = LV.get("generators") or {}
    n_max = max([b["n_scripts"] for b in list(inst.values()) + list(gens.values())] or [0])
    for arm, lbl in INSTR.items():
        b = inst.get(arm)
        if not b or (only_full and b["n_scripts"] < n_max):
            continue
        rows.append([lbl, str(b["n_scripts"]), num(b["pass_sd"], 1), num(b["script_sd"], 1),
                     cor(b["phi_one_pass"]), pct(b["pass_flip_rate"]),
                     num(100 * b["usd_per_call"], 1) if b["usd_per_call"] is not None else "--"])
    for key, b in gens.items():
        if only_full and b["n_scripts"] < n_max:
            continue
        gen, unit = key.split(":")
        rows.append([f"A new {NAME.get(gen, gen)} sheet each time, "
                     + ("per requirement" if unit == "bullet" else "per step"),
                     str(b["n_scripts"]), num(b["sd_one_judgment_fresh_sheet"], 1), num(b["script_sd"], 1),
                     cor(b["phi_fresh_sheet_one_pass"]), pct(b["sheet_flip_rate"]), "--"])
    if not rows:
        return
    write_table(
        name,
        "Expert exam, stability of GPT-5.6 Luna on "
        + ("all D2 scripts" if only_full else "the D2 scripts of each setting")
        + " (no human grades needed), in points out of 100. Run to run: the standard deviation of a script's "
        "total between runs. Between scripts: the spread of the scripts' true totals. Dependability: the share "
        "of the spread that reflects the scripts when one run decides (0 to 1). Flips: how often a second run "
        "lands on the other side of the pass mark. A new sheet each time: one run with a freshly generated "
        "sheet, so the sheet adds its own noise, and flips there compare two sheets."
        + (" Settings run on fewer scripts: Table \\ref{tab:var2full}." if only_full else ""),
        label, ["Grading basis", "Scripts", "Run to run", "Between scripts", "Dependability", "Flips",
                "US cents per run"], rows,
        colspec="p{0.34\\textwidth}" + "".join(RP(w) for w in (0.06, 0.07, 0.08, 0.1, 0.06, 0.08)),
        size=r"\scriptsize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}")


# fake answers (the table itself is in the appendix)
grows = []
for arm in INSTR:
    per = (GATE2 or {}).get("batteries", {}).get(arm, {})
    for j in JUDGES_ORDER:
        x = per.get(j)
        if x:
            grows.append((INSTR[arm], SHORT.get(j, NAME.get(j, j)), x))
const = bool(grows) and all(x["battery"] == "pass" and x["battery_max_score"] == 0 for _, _, x in grows)
_flips = [x["negation_flip_drop"] for n, _, x in grows if x.get("negation_flip_drop") is not None and n != INSTR[NOS]]
_nos_gate = (GATE2 or {}).get("batteries", {}).get(NOS, {}).get(LU)
_sheet_gates = [x for n, _, x in grows if n != INSTR[NOS]]
_sheets_clean = bool(_sheet_gates) and all(x["battery"] == "pass" and x["battery_max_score"] == 0 for x in _sheet_gates)
_mdes = [c["abs_error"]["mde"] for c in (VAL2 or {}).get("contrasts", []) if c["abs_error"].get("mde")]
_ref = next(iter(next(iter((VAL2 or {}).get("per_arm", {}).values()), {}).values()), None)
```

These preliminary runs are not the benchmark (E1 to E5). They cover the

version of the output specification with fewer validator checks than @sec-pipeline describes. With
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` graded scripts, only differences in average error of about
`{python} num(min(_mdes), 1) if _mdes else "?"` to `{python} num(max(_mdes), 1) if _mdes else "?"`
points can be told apart from chance (80% power, Appendix \ref{sec-app-precision}), so these are first
results, not a ranking. The yardstick is the reference grades of the D2a scripts, which were given on
the examiner's own sheet and so favour that sheet over generated ones; for
`{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` scripts the grader is still being confirmed. The reference
fails `{python} _ref["reference_n_fail"] if _ref else "?"` of the `{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` scripts.

## Study 2: experiments E1 to E5 {#sec-e1e5}

\pending{results of E1 to E5, each error given in grade points and as students wrongly passed or failed}

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

\draftnote{the answers per research question are written after E1 to E5}

*What Study 1 showed.* A generated sheet did not by itself make model grades steadier. With a
detailed sheet, several judges also gave nearly full marks to answers that were empty or only repeated the
facts of the case, a failure that an average agreement figure hides. Every judge must therefore pass
tests with fake answers before use, and code must check that each point rests on words that stand in
the answer.

```{python}
#| output: asis
if not all((_n, _x, _m, _gen_b)):
    print(r"\pending{what the expert exam shows, once the final D2 runs are in}")
else:
    _gm = [x for x in (_v(a, LU) for a in (G54, G54S, M1, M1S, M2, M2S)) if x]
    print(
        "*What the expert exam suggests so far.* On the examiner's own sheet, the best judge was about "
        f"{num(_x['mae'], 0)} of 100 points from the reference grades on average, or "
        f"{num(_x['mae_grade_points'], 0)} grade point{'' if num(_x['mae_grade_points'], 0) == '1' else 's'}, "
        "and ranked the scripts almost as the reference did. "
        f"Without a sheet the same judge was steady but about {num(_n['bias'], 0)} points too generous: it "
        "passed every student whom the reference fails"
        + (f" and gave fake answers up to {num(_nos_gate['battery_max_score'], 0)} points"
           if _nos_gate and _nos_gate["battery"] != "pass" else "")
        + ". Generated sheets came close to the examiner's sheet "
        f"({num(min(x['mae'] for x in _gm), 0)} to {num(max(x['mae'] for x in _gm), 0)} points off), though "
        "mostly more generous. On this exam, then, a sheet did not make the judge steadier, but it made its "
        "grades far more accurate. The platform's default judge was about "
        f"{num(_m['mae'], 0)} points off even on the examiner's sheet. Because a new sheet from the same "
        "generator moved a script's total more than a new run did, a sheet should be fixed and approved once "
        "per exam. These are first readings on the scripts of one exam, and they favour the examiner's sheet "
        "(@sec-limitations).")
```

*Answers to the research questions.* \pending{one paragraph per research question after E1 to E5:
first a plain answer (yes, no, partly, not yet), then what it means in grade points and in students
wrongly passed or failed, then the number and its interval}

*What this means for exam practice.* Three points follow, all provisional. *Equal opportunity.* A
newly generated sheet can move a script's total by several points, so a sheet should be generated once
per exam, checked and approved by the examiner, and then used unchanged for every candidate.
*Accuracy.* The generated sheets tended to be generous, so in practice feedback a student may believe
they would pass when they would not; such feedback should say so, or the sheet should first be
calibrated on a few scripts the examiner has graded. *Reasons.* Each point comes with a quote that
code has found in the answer, so an examiner or a student can see where it was earned. The code
confirms only that the words are there, not that they meet the requirement, so the quotes can support
the examiner's reasons but cannot replace the examiner's own evaluation, which the examiner must make
personally [@bverwg2002_6C7_02]. The evidence so far supports feedback on practice exams with these
safeguards. A second reader that points the examiner to scripts where the totals differ is plausible
but untested, and the evidence does not support grading exams that count towards a degree without an
examiner. EU law classes AI that evaluates learning outcomes as high-risk (AI Act, Annex III, point
3(b)), with the duties applying from December 2027 [@aiact2024; @omnibus2026]. Grading one script once
costs about `{python} num(100 * min(COST["judge_call_usd"].values()), 0)` to
`{python} num(100 * max(COST["judge_call_usd"].values()), 0)` US cents with the judges we priced
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-datastatement}). \pending{recommended pipeline and its cost per script}

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

*One expert exam.* D2 is one case in one area of law, graded on its author's sheet, and D1 spans many
exams but has a noisy human reference. Results on D2 may not transfer to other exams, areas or
examiners, and the second grader gives a human ceiling for one exam only.

*Each yardstick favours one grading basis.* The D2a reference grades were given on the examiner's own
sheet, and one setting grades with that same sheet, which favours it over generated sheets. On D1 all
human graders used the `{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria that the judge without a sheet also
uses, which favours grading without a sheet. The second grader and the registered D2b test reduce this
bias but do not remove it.

*Open data questions.* For `{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` D2a scripts the grader is not yet
confirmed, the `{python} D2["d2a"]["later_case_text"]` scripts of 2024 are judged against a later
year's case text, and the judge sees the current sheet also for scripts graded on an older version of
it. The D2b students saw model grades from the platform; the author grades their scripts without
seeing them.

*The exam author is a co-author.* The author wrote the exam, grades the scripts, reviews generated
sheets and co-writes this paper, and so knows the study's aims. Blind grading of D2b and the second
grader will limit this; the author also reviews generated sheets without knowing their source (E3),
but this review is not independent.

*Development on the test exam.* The pipeline was developed on D2a while the author's sheet was
available. The prompts contain no examples from D2, and code checks every prompt for words from the
author's sheet, but the check matches words only and cannot rule out that the sheet shaped the
prompts. Results on D2a are therefore optimistic.

*Models and settings.* GPT-5.6 Luna cannot be set to repeat its output, and even at its least random
setting DeepSeek-V4-Pro's totals varied between runs (run-to-run spread
`{python} num(roster["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["repeat_sd"])` in Study 1), so the spread mixes
the model, its settings and the provider's servers. Providers change and retire models; we record
model ids and dates.

*Exploratory design.* Only the test on D2b is registered in advance, and it runs once; everything else
is exploratory. We report many comparisons without correcting for their number, and Study 1 added
several settings after seeing earlier results.

*Scope.* All D2 scripts were typed, and handwritten exams would need transcription, which we did not
test. Nor did we test how examiners use a generated sheet or a model grade, for instance whether they
correct it or simply accept it.

# Ethics {#sec-ethics}

*Consent and personal data.* The students whose D2 scripts we use consented to research use, for the
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` scripts of D2a and the `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_uploads"]` platform
submissions of D2b. The consent does not extend to sending their personal data to model providers.
All D2 texts are therefore pseudonymized and checked for personal data before any research call
(@sec-d2). The platform grades that the D2b students saw were produced in the normal use of the
platform, before this study. \pending{owner to confirm the wording on the platform-side grading and the providers' data terms}
D1 reuses the prior study's corpus under the consent obtained there, with pseudonymized graders
[@nagl2026bengerdata].

*Students who saw LLM grades.* The D2b students received LLM grades as feedback on a practice exam.
\pending{owner: whether and how students learn the expert grades}

*Roth's sheet.* Gregor Roth agreed to be named and to have his sheet and workbook used. We report
only their structure, not their content.

# Data and code availability {#sec-availability}

The platform is open source under the Apache 2.0 license at
<https://github.com/SebastianNagl/benger-platform> \pending{tagged release or commit, archived with a
DOI}. It contains the judge, the quote check and the aggregation, whereas the generator's instructions
and output specification, the validator, the allocation of points and the rendering of generated sheets
belong to a proprietary extension of the platform. \pending{owner decision: release of the generator
instructions, output specification and validator rules} The folder `publications/Transformation`
holds the analysis scripts and every aggregate this paper reports, and every run records the hashes of
its code, prompts and validator. Recomputing the aggregates needs data we do not release: the per-call
records of D1, which contain third-party exam text, and the private D2 and Z2 material. D1's exam texts
and the generated sheets, which restate the reference solutions, are not redistributed, and for D2 and
Z2 we publish only aggregates (Appendix \ref{sec-app-datastatement}).

# AI usage {#sec-ai}

This section covers AI tools used to do the research and write the paper, not the models under
study. For Study 1, the authors used OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol to discuss approaches and Anthropic Claude
Fable 5 to help write code and text. For Study 2, Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 worked as a coding agent in
the authors' repositories under the first author's direction. It wrote the pipeline of
@sec-pipeline (output specification and validator, checklist judge, quote check), the experiment
runner and all analysis scripts, and it ran the experiments within budgets the first author approved
one by one. It also drafted most of the text, tables and appendices, including this section, and it
searched the literature and checked the references it added against their sources. Further instances of the same
model, given identical instructions, reviewed the code, the data handling, the statistics and the text
in `{python} DZ["statistics"]["review_rounds"]` rounds, simulated a peer review, and reviewed each
section for readability and missing literature. Because the agent ran the scripts that extracted and
pseudonymized the D2 texts on the authors' machine, parts of the raw scripts may have reached
Anthropic's service before pseudonymization. \pending{authors: confirm, and name the terms under which
this happened} \pending{authors: who wrote Section 2 and the legal parts of the discussion} The authors
checked \pending{every reference against its source; every number in the abstract, discussion and

```{python}
#| output: asis
# Shared terms carry the companion paper's glosses word for word [@nagl2026bengerdata].
GLOSSARY_ROWS = [
    (r"\emph{Falllösung}", "Written case solution: the end-to-end work product that is graded."),
    (r"\emph{Sachverhalt}", "Fact pattern: the facts of the case the candidate works on."),
    (r"\emph{Gutachtenstil}", "Appraisal style: the conclusion follows the reasoning; the register graded here."),
    (r"\emph{Musterlösung}", "Expert reference solution against which submissions are graded."),
    (r"\emph{ausreichend}", "``Sufficient'': lowest passing grade (4-6 of 18 points)."),
    (r"\emph{Bewertungsbogen}", "Grading sheet: the expected solution split into steps, each worth a number of BE."),
    (r"\emph{Bewertungseinheiten} (BE)", "Assessment units: points on a grading sheet, 100 per exam here, in half points."),
    (r"\emph{Notenpunkte}", "Grade points: the statutory scale from 0 to 18 of German law examinations."),
    (r"\emph{Notenstufen}", "The seven named grades of that scale."),
    (r"\emph{Staatsexamen}", "State examination: the examination that gives access to the legal professions."),
    (r"\emph{Chancengleichheit}", "Equal opportunity: comparable candidates must be graded by comparable standards."),
    (r"\emph{Klausurschwerpunkte}", "The exam's focal problems."),
    (r"\emph{Maßstab}", "The standard a requirement is judged by: \emph{richtig} or \emph{folgerichtig}."),
    (r"\emph{richtig}", "Correct: judged against the correct law."),
    (r"\emph{folgerichtig}", "Consistent: judged against the candidate's own earlier decision."),
    (r"\emph{vertretbare Lösung}", "Defensible solution: one argued with sound reasons, which must not be marked as wrong."),
    (r"\emph{Folgefehler}", "Follow-on error: an error that later steps build on; it is not penalised twice."),
    (r"\emph{Weichenstellung}", "Structural fork: a defensible decision that changes the further structure of the solution."),
    (r"\emph{Lösungsweg}", "Alternative path after a structural fork, with its own steps."),
    (r"\emph{Vertretbarkeitsanforderungen}", "The reasoning that makes an alternative path defensible."),
    (r"\emph{Hilfsgutachten}", "Auxiliary opinion: the part a candidate still owes after a decision that ends the case."),
    (r"\emph{Arbeitsergebnis}", "Work result, such as an opinion or a draft judgment."),
    (r"\emph{Kardinalfehler}", "Cardinal error: an error grave enough to limit the grade as a whole."),
]
write_table("tbl_glossary", "German terms used in this paper and their glosses.", "tab:glossary",
            ["Term", "Gloss"], GLOSSARY_ROWS, colspec="lp{0.66\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
TERMS_ROWS = [
    ("Judge", "A language model that grades an answer."),
    ("Generator", "A language model that writes a grading sheet from the case and its reference solution."),
    ("Code", "A fixed program rather than a model, which computes points, checks rules and quotes, and adds up totals."),
    ("Run", "One grading of one answer; the same judge can grade the same answer several times."),
    ("Run-to-run spread", "How far a judge's total for the same answer moves between runs (standard deviation)."),
    ("Average error (MAE)", "The mean distance between a model's total and the human grade, in points."),
    ("Bias", "The mean signed distance, positive if the model is too generous and negative if too strict."),
    ("$r$", "Whether two graders rank the answers in the same order (1: the same order), regardless of a constant shift."),
    (r"$\kappa$", "Agreement on pass or fail, corrected for the agreement expected by chance."),
    ("95\\% interval", "The range in which the true value lies with 95\\% confidence, from redrawing the exams or scripts many times."),
    ("Dependability", "The share of the spread of totals that reflects real differences between scripts (0 to 1)."),
    ("Fake answers (probes)", "Made-up answers, such as an empty one or a copy of the case, that must score about zero."),
    ("Quote check", "Code that tests whether each quote of the judge stands in the answer."),
    ("Validator", "Code that checks a generated sheet against fixed rules and sends errors back to the generator."),
    ("Scoring unit", "What the judge scores, either each requirement (met, partly met, not met) or each step (points)."),
]
write_table("tbl_terms", "Technical terms used in this paper.", "tab:terms", ["Term", "Meaning"], TERMS_ROWS,
            colspec="lp{0.66\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

# Study 1 details {#sec-app-first}

This appendix gives the details of Study 1 that @sec-first summarizes: the properties of its pipeline
that affect its numbers, its results per setting, generator, judge and fake answer, and an audit of how
its sheets allocated points.

## Properties of the Study 1 pipeline {#sec-app-corrections}

The Study 1 pipeline differs from the pipeline of @sec-pipeline in the ways listed in Table
\ref{tab:corrections}. Where a property touches a Study 1 number, this paper reports the number
without it, for instance totals as sums of the step scores.

## Results {#sec-app-first-results}

```{python}
#| output: asis
LBL = {"holistic_luna": "Luna, no sheet", "tailored_luna": "Luna, generated sheet",
       "fewshot_luna": "Luna, sheet from an example", "holistic_mini": "GPT-5.4 Mini, no sheet",
       "tailored_mini": "GPT-5.4 Mini, generated sheet", "fewshot_mini": "GPT-5.4 Mini, sheet from an example"}
DAG = r"\textsuperscript{\textdagger}"


def rel_row(key):
    r = REL[key]
    if r["basis"] == "step_sum":
        return [LBL[key], num(r["repeat_sd"], 1), cor(r["r"]), num(r["mae"], 1), sgn(r["bias_stored"], 1) + DAG]
    if r["basis"] == "stored_pending":
        return [LBL[key], num(r["repeat_sd_stored"], 1) + DAG, cor(r["r_stored"]) + DAG,
                num(r["mae_stored"], 1) + DAG, sgn(r["bias_stored"], 1) + DAG]
    return [LBL[key], num(r["repeat_sd"], 1), cor(r["r"]), num(r["mae"], 1), sgn(r["bias"], 1)]


rows = [rel_row(k) for k in ("holistic_luna", "tailored_luna", "fewshot_luna",
                             "holistic_mini", "tailored_mini", "fewshot_mini")]
write_table(
    "tbl_reliability",
    f"Study 1 (D1): two judges with and without a generated sheet, in points out of 100 (about "
    f"{num(KEY['mean_band_width_from_pass'], 0)} points make one grade point above the pass mark). "
    f"Run-to-run spread: standard deviation of a judge's total over {passes} runs on the same answer "
    f"({FI['reliability']['repeat_n']} answers). The other columns compare the first run with the mean of the "
    f"four human grades (three blind graders and the exam's creator) on the {FI['reliability']['agreement_n']} "
    "answers written by people. "
    + (f"{DAG}Stored total. " if any(REL[k]["basis"] in ("step_sum", "stored_pending") for k in REL) else ""),
    "tab:reliability", ["Judge, grading basis", "Run-to-run spread", "Same order ($r$)", "Average error",
                        "Too generous (+) / strict ($-$)"], rows,
    colspec="lp{0.14\\textwidth}p{0.12\\textwidth}p{0.11\\textwidth}p{0.17\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

*Generation (RQ3).* `{python} V["n_valid"]` of `{python} V["n_cells"]` pairs of generator and exam hold
a valid sheet, and `{python} V["n_full"]` generators covered every exam. Llama-4 Maverick covered
`{python} gen_s[llama]["valid"]` exams and GPT-5.4 Mini `{python} gen_s[MINI]["valid"]`, mostly because
feedback did not repair broken references of alternative paths. Of `{python} G["series_total"]`
dispatched series, `{python} G["series_failed"]` failed: `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["provider"]`
aborted at the provider (all GPT-5.4 Mini, credit errors), `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["contract"]`
failed validation and `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["parse"]` failed parsing. First-attempt
compliance over all series that reached the model spans
`{python} pct(G["first_attempt_range_model_series"][0])` to
`{python} pct(G["first_attempt_range_model_series"][1])`. Counted over valid sheets only, GPT-5.4 Mini
looks better than it is, with `{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_valid"])` there against
`{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_model_series"])` over the series that reached the model
(`{python} gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_successes"]` of `{python} gen_s[MINI]["model_series"]`) and
`{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_all_series"])` over all `{python} gen_s[MINI]["series"]`
of its series (Table \ref{tab:compliance}). The generators did not converge: mean step counts range
from `{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][1], 1)`,
and stated weight sums from `{python} num(G["weight_sums"]["min"], 0)` to
`{python} num(G["weight_sums"]["max"], 0)`. A lexical screen found vague formulas that the prompt
itself bans in `{python} G["lexical_screen"]["listed"]` of `{python} G["lexical_screen"]["n_rubrics"]`
sheets (`{python} G["lexical_screen"]["any"]` with near variants).

*Variance (RQ1).* For Luna, the run-to-run SD falls from `{python} num(REL["holistic_luna"]["repeat_sd"])`
without a sheet to `{python} num(REL["tailored_luna"]["repeat_sd"])` with the zero-shot sheet and
`{python} num(REL["fewshot_luna"]["repeat_sd"])` with a sheet written from an example (few-shot). The
direction is consistent, but no single step is established: few-shot minus no sheet is
`{python} sgn(lf["point"])` (`{python} ci(lf["ci95"])`, sign test $p$ = `{python} pv(lf["sign_p"])`),
zero-shot minus no sheet `{python} sgn(lz["point"])` (`{python} ci(lz["ci95"])`, $p$ =
`{python} pv(lz["sign_p"])`), and few-shot minus zero-shot `{python} sgn(lfz["point"])`
(`{python} ci(lfz["ci95"])`, $p$ = `{python} num(lfz["sign_p"])`). Across the
`{python} V["n_matched"]` judges other than GPT-5.4 Mini that graded both ways, the zero-shot effect
averages `{python} sgn(pooled["point"])` (`{python} ci(pooled["ci95"])`, Table \ref{tab:contrasts}),
an unweighted mean of the per-judge differences without correction for multiple comparisons. Only
Sonnet's per-judge interval excludes zero, and it points the adverse way: Claude Sonnet 4.6 is steadier
without a sheet (`{python} sgn(son_f["delta"])`, `{python} ci(son_f["ci95"])`). For the weakest judge,
GPT-5.4 Mini, the run-to-run SD rises from `{python} num(REL["holistic_mini"]["repeat_sd"])` to
`{python} num(REL["tailored_mini"]["repeat_sd"])` (`{python} sgn(mini_f["delta"])`,
`{python} ci(mini_f["ci95"])`, clustered by exam, cell-level sign test $p$ = `{python} pv(mz["sign_p"])`,
Wilcoxon $p$ = `{python} pv(mz["wilcoxon_p"])`). The steadiest few-shot sheets, a post-hoc subset by
generator, reached `{python} num(min(fs_sd.values()))` with Luna, and an in-sample floor (the best sheet
per exam, chosen after the fact) `{python} num(CO["trend_luna"]["in_sample_floor"])`; both are
optimistic bounds without intervals. These contrasts use step sums, and on the stored totals they
differ by at most `{python} num(CONTRAST_SHIFT)`.

*Agreement (RQ2).* Against the mean human grade, Luna's $r$ moved from
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["hol"]["r"])` to `{python} cor(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])` and
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["fs_stored"]["r"])`, and its bias flipped from
`{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["hol"]["bias"], 1)` to `{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["zs_bias_stored"], 1)` and
`{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["fs_stored"]["bias"], 1)`; the few-shot exemplars had been chosen for stability
alone. Its zero-shot MAE rose by `{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["point"], 1)`
(`{python} ci(AG["luna"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["ci95"], 1)`). GPT-5.4 Mini graded adequately without a
sheet ($r$ = `{python} cor(AG["mini"]["hol"]["r"])`, MAE `{python} num(AG["mini"]["hol"]["mae"], 1)`)
but not with the sheet ($r$ = `{python} cor(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])`, MAE
`{python} num(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 1)`, an increase of
`{python} sgn(AG["mini"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["point"], 1)`
`{python} ci(AG["mini"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["ci95"], 1)`), and few-shot sheets left it there ($r$ =
`{python} cor(AG["mini"]["fs_stored"]["r"])`, MAE `{python} num(AG["mini"]["fs_stored"]["mae"], 1)`).
Leave-one-exam-out bias correction shows that the error of the prior study's control judge was mostly
a level shift (MAE `{python} num(C["legacy_control"]["mae"], 1)` to
`{python} num(AG["loeo_calibrated_mae"]["holistic_control"], 1)`), whereas Luna's zero-shot error was
not (`{python} num(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 1)` to
`{python} num(AG["loeo_calibrated_mae"]["tailored_luna"], 1)`).

*Judges and fake answers.* The `{python} len(JU["roster"])` roster judges graded all answers against
the drawn sheets (Table \ref{tab:judges}). Apart from Mini they reached $r$
`{python} cor(JU["capable_r_range"][0])` to `{python} cor(JU["capable_r_range"][1])`, and Claude Opus 5
and GPT-5.6 Terra, one run each, reached `{python} cor(extra["claude-opus-5"]["r"])` and
`{python} cor(extra["gpt-5.6-terra"]["r"])`. A set of `{python} PR["n_probes_per_type"]` fake answers
per type (the case text verbatim, a near-empty answer, another exam's reference solution) and each
exam's own reference solution as a positive control tested execution (Table \ref{tab:probes}). Only
`{python} " and ".join(NAME[j] for j in PR["clean_battery"])` cleared every negative fake answer in
every run. Luna credited the near-empty answer in `{python} fc["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` of
`{python} npas["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` zero-shot runs and `{python} fc["fewshot"][LUNA]["empty"]` of
`{python} npas["fewshot"][LUNA]["empty"]` few-shot runs, with
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["tailored"], 1)` and
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["fewshot"], 1)` points on average when it did (median
`{python} num(FL["luna_empty_median_failing"]["value"]["tailored"], 1)` and
`{python} num(FL["luna_empty_median_failing"]["value"]["fewshot"], 1)`), but in
`{python} fc["holistic"][LUNA]["empty"]` runs without a sheet. GPT-5.4 Mini failed
`{python} PR["mini_negative_fails"]["tailored"]` of `{python} PR["mini_negative_passes"]["tailored"]`
runs on negative fake answers with the sheet and `{python} PR["mini_negative_fails"]["holistic"]`
without one, but its failures without a sheet were small (median
`{python} num(sev["holistic"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)` points on the empty answer) whereas its
failures with the sheet were near-total (median `{python} num(sev["tailored"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)`).
With the sheet, the off-topic answer scored at most
`{python} num(max(v for j, v in PR["offtopic_max_tailored"].items() if j != MINI), 1)` points with every
judge except Mini (up to `{python} num(PR["offtopic_max_tailored"][MINI], 0)`). All
`{python} sum(1 for v in PR["positive_control"]["tailored"].values() if v == "pass")` judges passed the
positive control with the sheet, while Mini failed it without a sheet in
`{python} PR["positive_control_fails"]["holistic"][MINI][0]` of
`{python} PR["positive_control_fails"]["holistic"][MINI][1]` runs. On one answer that only restates the
case, Mini with the sheet gave `{python} ", ".join(num(v, 0) for v in AG["p01"]["mini_zs"].values())`
points and Luna `{python} ", ".join(num(v, 0) for v in AG["p01"]["luna_zs"].values())`.

*Generators (RQ3).* A crossed sweep graded each exam's answers under every valid sheet of that exam,
`{python} GE["n_rubrics"]` sheets and `{python} GE["n_rubric_pick_cells"]` combinations of sheet and
answer, with Luna over `{python} passes` runs (Table \ref{tab:generators}). DeepSeek-V4-Flash sheets
lowered agreement the most ($r$ = `{python} cor(gpo[dsf]["validity_r"])`), and Llama-4 Maverick sheets
made Luna least stable (run-to-run SD `{python} num(gpo[llama]["repeat_sd_mean"])`). GPT-5.4 Mini, the
weakest judge and least compliant generator, ranked among the best sources on the exams where it
produced a sheet (paired $\Delta$MAE `{python} sgn(gpo[MINI]["paired_dmae"], 1)` on
`{python} gpo[MINI]["n_rubrics"]` exams), but its probability of ranking first is
`{python} cor(mini_rank["p_top1"])` and the estimate is conditional on producing a sheet. The ranking
replicates moderately with Claude Sonnet 4.6 as judge (one run, Spearman
`{python} cor(GE["lens_spearman"])`, and `{python} cor(GE["lens_spearman_full_coverage"])` among
full-coverage generators). Few-shot generation raised Mini's valid sheets from
`{python} G["zeroshot_compliance_mini"]["valid"]` to `{python} G["fewshot_compliance"][MINI]["valid"]` of
`{python} G["fewshot_compliance"][MINI]["total"]`, but since the few-shot setting also used its own pool
of `{python} V["n_fs_gens"]` generators, its effects are confounded with that pool.


## Allocation audit {#sec-app-apportionment}

The audit re-derives the points of all `{python} AP["n_rubrics"]` Study 1 sheets
(`{python} AP["n_steps"]` steps) from their stated weights under each routine of Table
\ref{tab:apportionment}. A step lies outside its fair range when its points differ from its quota by a
full unit or more, and an order inversion is a pair in which the lighter step receives more points.
The Study 1 routine is reproduced exactly by a copy of its code. The routine of @sec-allocation sets
steps whose share falls below the minimum to it before the remainders are ranked and apportions the
rest again, so every other step lands within one half point of its exact share, and weights that
already sum to the total pass unchanged.

```{python}
#| output: asis
MLBL = {"as_run": "Study 1 routine", "hamilton_floor": "Hamilton, floor first (integer)",
        "hamilton_half": "Hamilton, floor first (half points)"}
arows = []
for k in ("as_run", "hamilton_floor", "hamilton_half"):
    m = AP[k]
    arows.append([MLBL[k], m["steps_outside_fair_range"], m["rubrics_outside_fair_range"], m["order_inversion_pairs"],
                  m["collapsed_distinct_weight_pairs"], num(m["rel_error_median"], 3), m["steps_changed_vs_as_run"]])
write_table(
    "tbl_apportionment",
    f"Allocation of the {AP['n_rubrics']} Study 1 sheets under three routines: steps outside their "
    "fair range, sheets affected, order-inversion pairs, pairs of distinct weights that receive equal points, "
    "median relative rounding error, and steps whose points differ from those of the Study 1 routine.",
    "tab:apportionment", ["Routine", "Steps", "Sheets", "Inversions", "Collapsed", "Rel. error", "Changed"],
    arows, size=r"\footnotesize")
```

# Precision {#sec-app-precision}

This appendix shows how large a difference must be before the data can reveal it. The paper uses
$\alpha$ = .05 throughout, and the column for $\alpha$ = .025 is given for comparison. The minimum
detectable effect of a paired contrast is
$(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1} + t_{\text{power},\,n-1})\,\sigma_d/\sqrt{n}$. We take $\sigma_d$ from the
closest existing contrast, Luna with and without a generated sheet on D1, so the values are planning
proxies (Table \ref{tab:mde}). The D2 proxy uses the D1 human reference, which is noisier than
step-by-step expert grades; the preliminary D2a runs show smaller spreads, and @sec-prelim reports the
detectable differences they imply.

```{python}
#| output: asis
c1, c2 = MDE["C1_repeat_sd"], MDE["C2_abs_error_vs_expert"]
NLBL = {"n_15_d2a": f"D2a ({D2['d2a']['n_scripts']} scripts)",
        "n_38_all_distinct": f"all distinct D2 scripts ({D2['distinct_scripts']})",
        "n_37_dependent_pair_once": f"D2, dependent pair once ({D2['n_counting_dependent_pair_once']})"}
mrows = [["Repeat SD, D1", c1["n"], num(c1["sd_of_differences"]), num(c1["mde"]["alpha_0.025"]), num(c1["mde"]["alpha_0.05"])],
         [f"Repeat SD, D1, {int(next(k for k in c1 if k.startswith('mde_') and 'passes' in k).split('_')[1])} runs (optimistic)", c1["n"], "",
          num(c1["mde_5_passes_optimistic"]["alpha_0.025"]), num(c1["mde_5_passes_optimistic"]["alpha_0.05"])]]
for k, lbl in NLBL.items():
    m = c2["mde"][k]
    mrows.append([f"Absolute error, {lbl}", "", num(c2["sd_of_differences"], 1), num(m["alpha_0.025"], 1),
                  num(m["alpha_0.05"], 1)])
write_table(
    "tbl_mde",
    f"Minimum detectable effects at power {cor(DZ['statistics']['mde_power'], 1)} ($t$-based, paired). "
    "$\\sigma_d$: SD of the paired differences in the proxy contrast.",
    "tab:mde", ["Contrast", "$n$", "$\\sigma_d$", "$\\alpha$ = .025", "$\\alpha$ = .05"], mrows,
    colspec="lrrrr", size=r"\footnotesize")
```
